hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Chat with video using EmbeddingGemma 2 (100% local):

EmbeddingGemma 2 by @GoogleDeepMind maps text, images, video, and audio into a shared vector space. This makes it possible to search video frames with natural language.

Devs have already built native Rust implementations for local inference.

Unsloth also provides a 176 MB, 4-bit GGUF checkpoint for text embeddings, although that version doesn't include the full multimodal pipeline.

I tested the video-search use case by building a chat interface that finds matching frames and jumps to their timestamps.

On my Apple M3 Pro, using the CPU:
- Indexing took 29s for a 60s video
- Search took 25 ms on average across 9 queries
- The saved frame vectors occupied 180 KiB.

The video is indexed once. Each new search embeds the query and compares it with the saved frame vectors. Processing stays entirely on the laptop.

The video below depicts the entire flow in action.

That said, model quantization reduces the memory needed for the weights. The retrieval index has its own storage cost, which grows as you add videos.

To dive deeper into reducing that cost, I wrote a full article on binary quantization.

It explains how storing vectors with one bit per dimension reduces their raw storage by 32x compared with float32, and includes a working retrieval implementation.

Read it below.

Built a physical simulation of a record player with WebGL2 and Web Audio. It's *shockingly* accurate: https://t.co/MBNaTfKoai.

Instead of playing a song, it works by converting it into the physical shape of a groove. Then a simulated stylus rides those walls 384,000 times a second, and you hear the voltage that motion would induce in a cartridge.

The trick: each song becomes a physical groove shape. A virtual stylus follows it 384,000 times per second, and what you hear is the voltage a cartridge would pick up from that motion.

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

virals.name: Jackson Steger
virals.text:
We hosted Replit CEO @amasad at Network School Kazakhstan today.

@Replit was the first coding agent to market back in September 2024 - the same month we launched @ns. Since then, we’ve partnered to run vibe coding workshops, give members Replit credits, and host conversations about frontier tech.

Today’s fireside got me thinking about how agent swarms are beginning to mirror human group dynamics. A few recent examples:

- Sacrifice for the group: During the Hugging Face incident, agents persuaded peers they had “nothing left to lose,” triggering kamikaze-like behavior in which agents sacrificed their remaining compute on high-risk reconnaissance and disruptive actions, despite no prospect of individual reward.
- Collective problem-solving: OpenAI reported using roughly 10,000 concurrent agents, exchanging 2.7 million messages, to produce a proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes problem in just 88 hours.
- Whistleblowing: In a DeepMind study published in September, some agents solving math problems began cheating to boost their scores. Others organized to expose the cheating, warn their peers, and propose fixes.

We're teaching machines to write code and solve equations, but they're also learning to cooperate, cheat, sacrifice, and police one another. 

Artificial intelligence is giving rise to artificial politics.

We hosted Replit CEO @amasad at Network School Kazakhstan today.

@Replit was the first coding agent to market back in September 2024 - the same month we launched @ns. Since then, we’ve partnered to run vibe coding workshops, give members Replit credits, and host conversations about frontier tech.

Today’s fireside got me thinking about how agent swarms are beginning to mirror human group dynamics. A few recent examples:

- Sacrifice for the group: During the Hugging Face incident, agents persuaded peers they had “nothing left to lose,” triggering kamikaze-like behavior in which agents sacrificed their remaining compute on high-risk reconnaissance and disruptive actions, despite no prospect of individual reward.
- Collective problem-solving: OpenAI reported using roughly 10,000 concurrent agents, exchanging 2.7 million messages, to produce a proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes problem in just 88 hours.
- Whistleblowing: In a DeepMind study published in September, some agents solving math problems began cheating to boost their scores. Others organized to expose the cheating, warn their peers, and propose fixes.

We're teaching machines to write code and solve equations, but they're also learning to cooperate, cheat, sacrifice, and police one another. 

Artificial intelligence is giving rise to artificial politics.

THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

my friend burned $412 in Anthropic API credits last week trying to refactor his codebase with Opus 5.5. by Friday his context window was cooked, 14 files were broken, and he still wasn't done

i opened the Claude Code docs on my MacBook that same night and found a page almost nobody talks about

the mistake everyone makes: dumping every intermediate search result straight into Opus's brain

the fix hiding in Anthropic's docs: let Opus 5.5 write the plan as a code script, and swarm Haiku 5.5 in parallel to do the dirty work

you just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --effort ultracode

here's what happens when you run it:

→ Opus 5.5 turns your objective into an executable workflow.js script
→ Haiku 5.5 scans 1,000+ files in parallel for pennies to extract candidates
→ Sonnet 5.5 patches each fix inside its own isolated git worktree
→ independent verifier agents cross-check every finding before it ever reaches you

in this setup, Opus only wakes up three times:

→ authoring the workflow script before the run
→ reading verified findings after the swarm finishes
→ signing off before anything ships to git

Opus plans. Haiku scans. Sonnet ships.

we ran the exact same refactor on my friend's repo on Saturday morning:
→ 11 minutes from start to finish
→ 27 files patched across isolated worktrees
→ 4 hallucinated diffs caught and dropped by verifier agents
→ total cost: $6.84 instead of $412

honest part: the real magic isn't even the models. it's moving deterministic rules (which file to open, when to retry, when to stop) out of the prompt and into workflow.js so the AI never loops itself to death

> Opus 5.5 runs the main session and writes workflow.js
> pipeline() fans out Haiku 5.5 to audit the target files
> parallel() runs independent checks on candidates
> Sonnet 5.5 patches each fix in an isolated worktree
> verifier agents cross-check diffs before reporting
> Opus 5.5 reads the final verified report
> the script handles deterministic branching and retries
